The decision in five points
  1. Whitbread's FY27 earnings are a cost trough, not a demand trough. The October 2026 Budget froze business rates, the April 2027 wage rise is the smallest in three years, and Whitbread's own restaurant exit and efficiency programme are already executed.
  2. Earnings per share should recover about 11% in FY28 (183p to 203p, level with consensus) and compound at about 12% a year to FY31, half from profit growth and half from buybacks funded by property sales.
  3. The share price return comes mainly from the multiple. At 12.6x two-year forward earnings the shares sit at the 22nd percentile of ten years; my fair multiple of 14.5x gives about +26% over twelve months, and the 16.6x guideline gives about +44%.
  4. The risk is a weak UK consumer. Each 1% of UK RevPAR (revenue per available room) moves EPS by about 4%, and lease-adjusted leverage of 3.4x sits just below the 3.5x limit; the bad case (30% probability) loses about 19%.
  5. Three dated reports settle the case: the Q3 trading update on 13-Jan-27, the FY27 results on 27-Apr-27 and the H1 FY28 results in October 2027.

#0The investment case

The one idea. Whitbread's earnings are a geared play on UK budget hotel room rates against a cost base set largely by the Chancellor. Whitbread is Premier Inn: an owner-operator of 86,700 UK budget hotel rooms (12% of all UK rooms and 34% of the economy and midscale segment) and 13,400 rooms in Germany. Premier Inn fills its UK rooms at 80% occupancy and an £88 average room rate, takes over 90% of UK bookings directly through its own website (so it pays no agency commission), and owns roughly half of the property underneath its hotels.

Whitbread's profits are highly geared to UK RevPAR because almost all of its costs are fixed (wages at 27% of sales, property, business rates and energy) and about 90% of its revenue is UK accommodation. Whitbread's competitive position therefore rests on its brand, its direct distribution and its scale, and its main risk is a fall in UK hotel demand or room prices.

The change. Three forces have turned in Whitbread's favour in the last six months, and each is large relative to a £410m annual profit base.

1. The cost cycle that crushed estimates has reversed.

Consensus FY27 adjusted EPS fell 17% over twelve months to 179p during the cost squeeze. The October 2026 Budget then froze English business rates in real terms for two years, which cuts Whitbread's expected FY28 and FY29 rates bill by £45 to 60m cumulatively (9 to 12% of FY29 consensus PBT). The National Living Wage rise for April 2027 is 3.9%, against 6.7% and 4.1% in the two prior years. Whitbread is on track for £60m of efficiencies this year after £83m last year, so its net UK cost inflation falls to 3 to 4%.

2. Whitbread's self-help is real and already executed.

All 197 branded restaurants were closed in September 2026, 173 of the restaurant sites are sold, and 850 extension rooms are open. Management guides to a £30 to 40m PBT uplift in FY28 from the Accelerating Growth Plan (AGP, the restaurant-to-rooms programme) and £100m by FY31. Germany adds a guided £15 to 25m in FY28 after its first profitable year.

3. The governance overhang has cleared.

Shareholders defeated the activist investor Corvex's board nominee on 9-Nov-26, with 83% of votes against. Corvex's campaign nonetheless extracted a 15% hurdle rate on all growth capital, a £1bn cut in capital spending and £1.5bn of property recycling.

Not cleared: demand.

UK demand is the headwind that has not cleared. The UK consumer is weak (the house view rates Consumer discretionary Double Underweight), corporate travel managers expect Premier Inn's negotiated rates to fall 3.5% in 2027, and the two-year rates freeze creates a £65m cliff edge in FY30 if the government does not extend it. Premier Inn is nonetheless outperforming its market: its Q3 RevPAR is +3.2% against a flat-to-weak midscale market and +0.4% at Travelodge, independent hotels' share of budget rooms has shrunk from 53% to 46% in a decade, and hotel construction is constrained until 2028.

How the change reaches the financials. FY27 (the year to February 2027) is the earnings trough, and FY28 is the recovery year.

  • FY27, the trough: revenue is flat at about £2.9bn as the restaurant exit removes about £160m of food and beverage (F&B) sales; EBITDA is flat at about £1.05bn; adjusted PBT falls to about £412m (consensus £407m; the first half already beat consensus by £11m); and EPS falls 12% to about 183p.
  • FY28, the recovery: the rates freeze, the AGP uplift, Germany's maturity and 2% RevPAR growth lift the EBITDA margin from 36% to about 38%, PBT to about £452m (consensus £461m) and EPS by 11% to about 203p (consensus 203p).
  • FY29 and beyond: EPS reaches about 229p on my numbers against 240p consensus. Buybacks, paused this year, resume once lease-adjusted leverage is clearly below 3.5x and add 3 to 5% a year to EPS from FY29.

The sell-side has already moved its numbers: FY28 EPS consensus is up 9% in three months, target prices are up 12%, and the share of Buy ratings is up 10 points to 40%. What remains to move is the market's narrative, from "a UK cost squeeze on an asset-heavy hotelier" to "the cost cycle is over, the self-help is landing and cash returns are resuming". That shift in narrative depends on two reports: the Q3 update on 13-Jan-27 (RevPAR and FY28 cost guidance) and the FY27 results on 27-Apr-27 (FY28 guidance, property proceeds and any buyback).

The foundation. Whitbread's operating machine is excellent, but its capital allocation is unproven, and the new five-year plan is the test of that capital allocation. Overall, the business quality is medium-to-good.

  • Strengths: a brand with a 20-point quality lead over its nearest rival; an 86% repeat rate; direct distribution worth 10 to 15 points of margin against peers that depend on online travel agents (OTAs); a freehold estate valued at £5.5 to 6.4bn against a £4.7bn market value; an investment-grade balance sheet; and a stable chief executive and finance director who have met or beaten short-term guidance and delivered their efficiency targets.
  • Weaknesses: a decade of £2.6bn of growth capital spending produced a 2.8% earnings CAGR and shares that lagged the FTSE 350 Travel and Leisure index; Whitbread's ROIC of 11% trails the franchisors'; lease-adjusted leverage of 3.4x sits one notch below the 3.5x limit; and each sale-and-leaseback converts a freehold cushion into a fixed rent that makes the next downturn worse.

The setup. The case fits best as a cause for concern (CfC) clearing in a quality cyclical at trough-on-trough, leading to reversion to normal. The causes for concern (the cost squeeze, the activist, the restaurant losses and Germany's losses) are clearing; FY27 EPS of 183p, against 207p in FY26, is the trough; and the multiple of 12.6x sits at the 22nd percentile of its ten-year range.

  • Present in Whitbread's setup: the clearing cause for concern, trough earnings, a low multiple, and a market leader taking share from a weakened rival.
  • Missing from Whitbread's setup: the demand cycle is not at a trough. UK RevPAR is still growing, so Whitbread's trough is a cost trough, and a UK consumer downturn could create a second trough. The quality label is also contested, because the shift to leasehold raises operating gearing.
  • A secondary fit: a big corporate change driving an EPS step-up (the restaurant exit, property recycling and Germany). That step-up is back-ended and modest (about 11% a year), so it does not carry the case alone.

The reward and the skew. The skew is positive but not lopsided: reward outweighs risk roughly two to one, and the downside has a 30% probability because the case is geared to a UK consumer the house view rates Double Underweight.

  • If the case plays out: the 24-month-forward EPS the market prices rises from about 216p today to about 238p in a year (+10%), and the multiple moves from 13.0x on my numbers towards the 16.6x guideline (+28%). The return is about +44% including the 3.5% dividend yield. At my own fair multiple of 14.5x (see #11) the return is about +26%.
  • If the case fails because UK RevPAR goes flat: FY28 EPS falls to about 185p, the multiple returns to its 11x floor, and the shares lose about 25%.
  • Probability-weighted: the expected 18-month return is about +22% (see #12).

What has to be true. Three conditions must hold, and each has a dated test.

  1. UK RevPAR growth holds at 2% or better, with Premier Inn ahead of the market. Richard will know at the Q3 update on 13-Jan-27 (the first five weeks of Q3 were +3.2%; RevPAR growth below 1.5% breaks the FY28 profit bridge) and at the FY27 results on 27-Apr-27, where FY28 net cost inflation guidance of 3% or less would confirm that the cost cycle has turned.
  2. FY28 delivers the guided uplift. The H1 FY28 results in October 2027 should show adjusted PBT of £310m or more (H1 FY27: £287m), Germany in profit for the half, and the 750 FY27 extension rooms trading.
  3. Property proceeds of £400m or more land in FY27, and lease-adjusted leverage prints at 3.3x or below at February 2027, so that the board can announce a buyback at the April 2027 or October 2027 results. Proceeds below £300m, or leverage at 3.5x, would mean the five-year plan is funding itself with debt, and the narrative would stall.

The five judgements that move the shares most. UK RevPAR moves the shares most; the FY30 business rates cliff edge is the largest single EPS risk but the furthest away.

  1. UK RevPAR in FY28 (+2% assumed). Each 1% of UK RevPAR is worth about £17m of PBT and 7.6p of EPS (3.7% of FY28 EPS). Flat RevPAR takes FY28 EPS from 203p to about 188p (7.5)%; RevPAR growth of +3.5% takes it to about 214p (+5.5%). The multiple moves with RevPAR, so the share price effect is two to three times the EPS effect.
  2. The Accelerating Growth Plan uplift (+£45m of EBITDA in FY28 over FY27 assumed). A one-year slip to +£20m cuts FY28 PBT by £25m and EPS by about 11p (5.5)%. The AGP uplift is highly plausible because the restaurant closures are done and Whitbread owns the freeholds.
  3. Germany (+£18m in FY28 assumed). A German business stuck at breakeven removes about 8p of FY28 EPS (4)% and, more importantly, removes the "second engine" leg of the narrative that a 16x multiple needs.
  4. Property proceeds and the buyback (£400m of proceeds in FY27, a £100m buyback in FY28 and £250m in FY29 assumed). Proceeds slipping to £250m delay buybacks by a year, cost about 2% of FY29 EPS and keep leverage at 3.4 to 3.5x, where the credit rating rather than the equity story dictates capital allocation.
  5. The business rates cliff edge in FY30 (half of £65m assumed). The full £65m is worth 29p of EPS (12% of FY30 EPS), and the sell-side has barely modelled FY30. The rates cliff edge is the main reason my FY30 is a stall year, and it is why the 16.6x guideline multiple is hard to defend on 24-month-forward earnings once FY30 enters that window in 2028.

#1Tailwinds and headwinds in the operating environment

Evidence. The tailwinds are mostly legislated or structural; the headwinds are mostly about demand.

Tailwinds

  • Policy: the Budget of 28-Oct-26 froze English hospitality business rates in real terms for FY28 and FY29. Whitbread's rates payments now rise £7.5 to 12.5m a year instead of £35m, a cumulative saving of £45 to 60m and 9 to 12% of FY29 consensus PBT. The National Insurance threshold for 21 to 24 year-olds was doubled, and the April 2027 minimum wage rise of 3.9% is the smallest in three years.
  • Supply: UK independent hotels' share of budget rooms fell from 53% to 46% between 2015 and 2025, and independent supply has fallen 11% since 2019. Construction starts are low, and UK room supply is not expected to recover to pre-pandemic levels before 2028, so Premier Inn sets prices in a market that is losing capacity.
  • Competition: Travelodge, the nearest rival, grew Q3 RevPAR by 0.4% against Premier Inn's 2.3% in the same quarter, raised its cost inflation guidance to 5.5 to 6.5% (Whitbread: 3 to 4%), and is described by one industry expert as "challenged without a cash injection".
  • Demand data: leisure demand is resilient (occupancy 81.0% against 80.8%), London RevPAR grew 4.6% in H1, and UK consumer spending rose 2.3% in October, with hospitality and leisure spending up 3.5%. Regulation of short-term rentals in European cities is also tightening.

Headwinds

  • The macro view: the house environment view rates Consumer discretionary Double Underweight and Hotels, leisure and hospitality Underweight. European consumer confidence is weak and edging lower, UK growth for 2027 has been cut to 1.0%, Bank Rate is 4.0% and the 10-year gilt yields 5.3%.
  • Demand and pricing: UK leisure demand has split in two, with the bottom tenth of households growing hotel spending by only 4% since 2019. Corporate travel managers expect Premier Inn's negotiated rates to fall 3.5% in 2027, while global brands get +2.8 to 5.5%. UK midscale and economy hotel prices fell 12.6% in August.
  • Dated costs: English mayors can levy a 5% overnight visitor tax from 2028 (£7 to 9m of PBT); German inbound travel is soft and German minimum wages have risen by up to 19% in four years; and the business rates freeze expires after FY29, with a possible £65m cliff edge.
Tailwinds: legislated or structural
  • Business rates frozen in real terms, FY28 and FY29
  • National Insurance threshold for 21 to 24 year-olds doubled
  • Independents' share of budget rooms 53% → 46% (2015 to 2025); supply short of pre-pandemic until 2028
  • Travelodge Q3 RevPAR +0.4% vs Premier Inn +2.3%; its cost guide 5.5 to 6.5%
  • Leisure occupancy 81.0%; London RevPAR +4.6% in H1
Headwinds: mostly demand

  • UK 2027 growth cut to 1.0%; Bank Rate 4.0%; 10-year gilt 5.3%
  • Corporate negotiated rates expected (3.5)% in 2027
  • UK midscale and economy pricing (12.6)% in August
  • German minimum wage up to +19% in four years

Inference. The cost environment has turned from hostile to neutral for two years. The competitive environment is the best in a decade, because the cost shock that hurt Whitbread hurt its weaker rivals more. The demand environment is the open question: Whitbread's own reported demand is not deteriorating (RevPAR growth accelerated from 1.8% in Q1 to 3.2% in early Q3), but every external reading in the house view says the UK consumer is fragile.

So what. The case does not need demand growth; it needs demand not to fall.

  • At +2% RevPAR, the FY28 profit bridge works.
  • At 0% RevPAR, the FY28 bridge still roughly works on cost relief alone, but the multiple will not re-rate.
  • At (2)% RevPAR, operating gearing does its damage.

Redburn's counter-argument is that rates relief keeps weak independent hotels alive and so caps industry RevPAR. I give it limited weight, because the independents' binding problems are wages and refurbishment capital, which the rates freeze does not fix.

Where I differ from the market. The market has priced the rates relief (an average EPS upgrade of 11.5% at Jefferies and 6 to 11% at Morgan Stanley) but still treats Whitbread as a proxy for the UK consumer cycle, which is why the shares are flat over twelve months while the sector median is up 21%. I think the shrinking supply and the weakness of competitors make Premier Inn's RevPAR more defensible than the macro reading implies, as Premier Inn's outperformance of the market by 260bp in Q2 and 70 to 100bp in Q3 shows. I agree with the market that a genuine UK consumer downturn would overwhelm all of these advantages.

Conclusion. The operating environment has swung from a strong cost headwind to a modest net tailwind for FY28 and FY29; the UK consumer is the one unresolved risk, and the FY30 rates cliff edge is the one dated future headwind. The operating environment supports step 2 of the case (the change is real and large) and leaves the first condition of step 7 (UK RevPAR holding at 2% or better) genuinely open.

Score: 60, set by the Rater. The October 2026 Budget's real-terms freeze on business rates (a £45 to 60m saving, 9 to 12% of FY29 PBT), the smallest wage rise in three years, shrinking independent supply and a struggling Travelodge turn the cost environment from hostile to neutral and the competitive environment favourable. These tailwinds are legislated or structural, but they are offset by a weak UK consumer (house view Double Underweight), corporate rates expected to fall 3.5% in 2027, visitor levies from 2028 and a £65m rates cliff edge in FY30. Consensus sales growth at the 49th percentile confirms that the external lift is to margins, not to demand. The environment is a modest but real net positive, which sits just below Linea Directa's advanced pricing cycle and above OEM's mild recovery.

#2Internally-driven change forces

Evidence. The five-year plan reset in April 2026 is large and mostly executed at the operating level, but its financial results are still to be proved.

The plan (reset in April 2026 and extended by twelve months to absorb the rates hit)

  • Gross capital spending cut by £1bn to £2.5bn, under a 15% minimum ROCE hurdle on all growth capital (15 to 20% on the AGP).
  • £1.5bn of freehold recycling, taking the freehold share of the estate from 50% to 30 to 40%.
  • Germany's room target trimmed from 20,000 to 18,000, with the pipeline refocused on prime city centres under a new local leadership team.
  • 8,000 new UK rooms and £250m of cumulative efficiencies over FY27 to FY31.
  • Targets for FY31: £275m of incremental PBT, +500bp of group ROCE and £2bn of cumulative free cash flow for shareholder returns.

Execution so far

  • All 197 branded restaurants closed by September 2026, ahead of the original schedule; 173 sites sold; 850 extension rooms open, with 750 due in FY27.
  • £39m of the £60m FY27 efficiencies delivered in H1; the Opera Cloud hotel management system rolled out across the estate.
  • 1,800 German rooms opened in H1, including 1,300 acquired and integrated; German accommodation sales +31%.
  • The Dartmouth and hub Old Bailey sale-and-leasebacks completed at a 4.75% net initial yield; a £300m seven-year bond priced in November 2026 to pre-fund the May 2027 maturity; two Future Inns hotels (292 rooms) bought.
  • A refreshed board (a new Chair in September 2025, a new Audit Chair in January 2026, and Mark Allan of Land Securities as property non-executive director in October 2026) and the activist defeated.

Problems

  • The restaurant exit cut F&B sales by 37% and adds £10m of costs in FY27.
  • Adjusting items ballooned to £178m in H1 (£62m of five-year-plan impairments, £38m of AGP impairments and £33m of cash costs), and capitalised interest rose to £23m in FY26 from £8.7m.
  • 3,800 roles are going, and a former manager describes unpaid overtime and weakened supervisor morale.
  • Bernstein calculates that the extended AGP will earn a lower double-digit ROCE than the first tranche, and that fully capitalising leases reduces the true ROCE uplift to 100bp rather than 500bp.
  • Property proceeds were only £53m to October against a £450 to 500m full-year target.
  • The Restricted Share Plan paid out 65% of maximum through a period of negative shareholder returns; a Performance Share Plan replaces it from 2027.

Inference. Whitbread's internal change is large, concrete and mostly executed at the operating level (the closures, the systems and the efficiencies), which is where this management team has always been strong. The parts of the plan still to prove are financial: that property proceeds arrive at 4.75 to 5.5% yields while the gilt yields 5.3%, that the extension rooms earn 15% or more, and that Germany converts higher volume (occupancy +4 points) into higher price (room rates were down 5% in local currency).

So what. A change programme worth 20% of PBT gross, funded by Whitbread's own property sales, is a genuine EPS driver, and its near-term pieces (the FY28 AGP uplift of £30 to 40m and Germany's £15 to 25m) are the most plausible. The strongest counter-case is Bernstein's: that the ROCE uplift is largely an accounting shift from owned to leased hotels, and that the headline £275m ignores the roughly £100m of new fixed lease cost that property recycling creates. Bernstein's reading is fair for FY31 but not for FY28, and the FY28 uplift is what the market will price over the next twelve months.

Where I differ from the market. Consensus has adopted the FY28 uplift (PBT £461m), and I am a little below it because of the lease and interest drag. The market, by contrast, has not yet given credit for the resumption of buybacks, which is the next piece of internal change to arrive; the sector digest calls the "sell property and return cash" story "Big but not Early" at Whitbread.

Conclusion. Whitbread's corporate change forces are strong, well advanced in execution and back-ended in financial proof, and capital recycling is the component most exposed to slippage. The change forces support step 2 of the case and underpin step 3's FY28 recovery; they leave the third condition of step 7 (property proceeds and leverage) open.

Score: 67, set by the Rater. A large, funded and mostly executed programme: all 197 restaurants closed early, 173 sold, extension rooms open, £83m then £60m of efficiencies, capital spending cut by £1bn under a 15% hurdle, Germany at its first profit under new leadership, and the activist defeated. Management guides to £30 to 40m of PBT from the AGP plus £15 to 25m from Germany in FY28, about 12% of PBT. Against the programme, property proceeds are only £53m of £450 to 500m, adjusting items reached £178m, and Bernstein reads much of the ROCE uplift as an owned-to-leased accounting shift. The programme is largely a repair of a mature, capital-heavy model with some growth (8,000 UK rooms and Germany) and with its financial proof still to come, so it sits just above OEM and below Theon's pivot.

#3Value chain, business model, financial profile and management

Evidence. Whitbread is a best-in-class operator with a capital-heavy financial profile and a management team stronger on operations than on capital allocation.

  • Industry structure: the UK budget segment is consolidating around two brands. Premier Inn holds 34% of economy and midscale rooms (19% in 2006), and Travelodge is the lease-heavy number two. Germany's 996,000 hotel rooms are 68% independent, and no brand holds more than 3% (Motel One 29,000 rooms, B&B 24,000, Premier Inn 13,400 heading to 18,000).
  • Value chain: Whitbread operates hotels (a typical EBIT margin of 17%) and owns property; it does not franchise brands (60% EBIT margins, valued at 16 to 18x EV/EBITDA against 8 to 9x for owner-operators). Whitbread's EBIT margin of 21 to 23% is above operator norms because it owns its hotels and sells direct, bypassing the 10 to 25% online travel agent commissions that take 60% of European independents' bookings.
  • Barriers to entry: a £6bn estate; UK brand awareness above 90%; first place in YouGov's quality and value rankings, 20 points ahead of Travelodge; an 86% repeat rate; a corporate booking portal with 76,000 clients that brings in a quarter of revenue; a proprietary dynamic pricing engine; and standardised procurement.
  • Financial profile: FY26 revenue of £2,920m (flat); an EBITDA margin of 36%; adjusted PBT of £483m (flat); ROIC of 11.1% (IHG about 18%); capital spending at 24% of revenue (asset-light peers 4 to 6%); negative FY26 free cash flow on FactSet's definition after £656m of capital spending; lease liabilities of £4.6bn; lease-adjusted net debt of 3.4x EBITDAR (limit 3.5x); a Fitch BBB- rating, stable since May 2026; and no dividend growth since FY24.
  • Management: Dominic Paul (chief executive since January 2023; previously the Costa sale, the Domino's turnaround and Royal Caribbean China) and Hemant Patel (finance director since 2022, at Whitbread since 2018) hold 313% and 204% of salary in shares, against requirements of 300% and 200%. There have been no insider sales in twelve months, and the Chair has bought shares in the market. Nine of the eleven board members are independent. The culture is lean (one employee per three rooms), staff engagement is 73%, staff turnover is falling, and Whitbread has been a Top Employer for twelve years.
  • Against: the shares lagged the FTSE 350 Travel and Leisure index over ten years; £2.6bn of growth capital spending produced a 2.8% earnings CAGR; margins fell at both of the chief executive's previous employers; guidance on the rates headwind moved from £50m to £35m; and the quality of growth capital spending is only now being disciplined by a hurdle rate.

Inference. Whitbread is a high-quality operator inside a medium-quality financial model. Its brand, distribution and cost machine are best-in-class for an owner-operator, but owning hotels caps returns at a low-teens ROCE and leaves free cash flow hostage to the capital spending cycle. Management is strong on operations and communication and average on capital allocation to date, and it is now constrained, for the better, by hurdle rates, a leverage ceiling and a watchful shareholder register.

So what. Whitbread's foundation is good enough to carry a reversion-to-normal case, because reversion needs only the operating machine (pricing, cost control and share gains), not a change in the business model. The foundation is not good enough for a franchisor's multiple, and the fair multiple in #11 respects that limit.

Where I differ from the market. The market values Whitbread at a 46% discount to asset-light peers, and the sector digest observes that the market pays first for proof. I agree that the discount is structural, but I think the market underrates the quality of the UK operating franchise by comparing Whitbread with franchisors. Against Travelodge, Scandic (EBITDA margin 15%) or Melia (28%), Whitbread's 36% EBITDA margin, 11% ROIC and 90% direct booking are superior.

Conclusion. The industry structure is favourable and improving, the business model has a durable but capped advantage, the financial profile is average and constrained by leverage, and management is operationally dynamic with a capital allocation record still to be rebuilt. This assessment supports step 4 of the case as a medium-quality foundation, and it caps the ambition of the multiple in step 6.

Score: 61, set by the Rater. The qualitative parts are good: a consolidating UK budget segment with Premier Inn at 34% and rising, a brand with a 20-point quality lead, over 90% direct distribution, scale, and an operationally excellent management. The financial profile is weaker. ROIC is about 11% on the memo's basis (2.5% reported, 20th percentile); capital spending is 23% of revenue (94th percentile, a bad reading), free cash flow is negative (14th percentile) and net debt is 5.0x EBITDA. A decade of £2.6bn of growth capital spending earned a 2.8% earnings CAGR, so the return on new capital is poor, and demand is cyclical. Whitbread is a capped operating franchise inside a capital-heavy model, level with Helios Towers and below Carlsberg's goodwill-depressed but higher-return brewing position.

#4Guidance conservatism, sell-side management and the record of delivery

Evidence. Management sets short-term guidance conservatively and beats it modestly, but its medium-term guidance has been reset once and is back-ended.

  • For: H1 FY27 adjusted PBT of £287m beat consensus of £276m by 4%, and H1 EPS of 125.1p beat 122p. Management "maintained its full-year view", and Morgan Stanley nudged its estimates up for a second time. The chief executive describes conservative assumptions as appropriate given limited visibility. The FY27 cost inflation guidance (gross 6.5 to 7.5%, net 3 to 4%) has held. The £60m efficiency target follows £83m delivered against a £50m target in FY26, and £75m in FY25. Germany's first annual profit arrived on schedule.
  • Against: Bernstein notes that merely holding estimates "became unusual" over the past year, as consensus FY27 EPS fell 17% over twelve months before recovering 5% in the last three. The rates headwind guidance moved from £50m to £35m. Deutsche Bank notes that two-thirds of the £60m efficiencies were front-loaded into H1, and Redburn expects £10m of H1 cost phasing to reverse in H2. The five-year plan itself was reset and extended within a year of its first version, and property proceeds are heavily back-ended (£53m to October against £450 to 500m).

Inference. Whitbread's short-term guidance is set conservatively and beaten modestly, which is the pattern Richard looks for. Its medium-term guidance (the five-year plan) has been reset once and is back-ended, so the plan's credibility is being rebuilt rather than banked. Government policy, not management over-promising, drove the FY26 downgrade cycle, and government policy equally drove the October 2026 upgrade cycle.

So what. The FY28 guidance given in April 2027 is the bigger lever for the shares; the next two events (13-Jan-27 and 27-Apr-27) are otherwise set up for small beats and held guidance rather than big upgrades. Q3 RevPAR is running ahead of the 1.5% most brokers assume, but the H2 cost phasing limits the FY27 PBT upside to perhaps £5 to 10m. The brokers' FY28 PBT range is wide (£444m to about £470m), and management's own bridge (AGP +£30 to 40m, Germany +£15 to 25m, business rates rising only £7.5 to 12.5m) points to the upper half of that range.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side's median rating is Hold (five of thirteen brokers rate the shares Buy), and the Hold camp's reasoning is "back-end loaded, few catalysts". I think the market is under-weighting the April 2027 FY28 guidance as a catalyst, because it will be the first full-year guidance set after the rates freeze and the restaurant closures, and management's habit is to guide so that it can beat.

Conclusion. Current guidance is conservative, the short-term delivery record is good, and the medium-term record is being rebuilt after a policy-driven reset. The guidance record supports step 3 of the case (small FY27 beats and a credible FY28 guide) and strengthens the dating of step 7's proof points.

Score: 57, set by the Rater. Short-term guidance is set conservatively and beaten modestly: H1 PBT came in 4% above consensus, cost guidance has held, and efficiency targets were beaten in FY25 and FY26. Against this, consensus FY27 EPS fell 17% over twelve months, the rates headwind guide moved, the five-year plan was reset and extended within a year, and proceeds are heavily back-ended. The downgrades were mostly policy-driven, not the result of over-promising, but the medium-term record is being rebuilt. That record places Whitbread a little above CVS's H2-weighted reaffirmation and just below Renew's honest cut-and-beat.

#5Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage and feedback loops

Evidence. Whitbread combines real pricing power and high operating gearing with financial leverage close to its ceiling.

  • Pricing power: a £7.75 RevPAR premium to the UK economy and midscale market; a 5 to 15% room rate premium to Travelodge; Q2 outperformance of 260bp; room rates up 1.9% to £87.60 at 81% occupancy in H1; and the ability to pass visitor levies through to guests separately.
  • Operating leverage: 1% of UK RevPAR is worth £16.5 to 17m of PBT (Morgan Stanley), 3 to 5% of PBT (Redburn's two estimates) or 3.5% of EPS (Deutsche Bank). Wages are 27% of sales, and a 1% rise in the wage bill costs 0.3 points of margin before mitigation.
  • Financial leverage: lease-adjusted net debt of £3.6bn against EBITDAR of £1.07bn (3.4x); fully capitalised net debt to EBITDA near 5x. The £300m 2.375% bond matures in May 2027, and refinancing it at about 6% adds £11m a year of interest.
  • Cost-out: efficiencies of £83m, £60m and then about £50m a year. Integrated hotel dining carries an operating margin 10 points higher than separate restaurants. Robot vacuums run across 700 sites, alongside AI housekeeping scheduling and Apple Wallet digital keys.
  • Feedback loops: direct bookings (app bookings +43% in H1, bookings initiated by AI search +70%) lower the cost of acquiring guests, which funds competitive prices, which sustain occupancy, which deepens the data in the pricing engine. Separately, freehold sales fund extension rooms at a 15 to 20% ROCE, which raise EBITDA, which lowers leverage, which releases buybacks.
  • Against: 77% of lease liabilities carry inflation-linked rent reviews. Each £100m of sale-and-leaseback adds about £5 to 6m of cash rent and about 7.5% in reported P&L charge (depreciation and interest are front-loaded), so £1.5bn of sales adds roughly £100m of fixed cost by FY31. Germany relies on online travel agents, so its pricing power is weaker (German room rates fell 5% in H1).

Inference. Whitbread's business model converts a 2% RevPAR gain plus 2% room growth into roughly 8 to 10% PBT growth before buybacks, and buybacks at a 12 to 13x multiple add a further 3 to 5% to EPS. The same gearing means that a 2% RevPAR fall wipes out a year of self-help. The restaurant exit permanently raises the operating margin and removes the one part of the business with no pricing power, so Whitbread's gearing to RevPAR is now cleaner and slightly higher.

So what. At Whitbread, revenue growth leads to outsized profit growth, which is exactly what a reversion case needs now that costs have stopped rising faster than revenue. The strongest counter-case is that the shift to leasehold and the inflation-linked rents make the "normal" margin Whitbread reverts to structurally lower than the FY24 peak (when UK ROCE was 15.5%). I accept that counter-case: my FY31 PBT of about £549m is still below FY24's.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side disagrees with itself on the size of the gearing (3% to 5% of PBT per 1% of RevPAR); I use Morgan Stanley's £17m because it is the most recent and the most granular estimate. The market treats the gearing as a risk; over the next 18 months, with RevPAR positive and costs contained, I think the gearing is the mechanism of the upside.

Conclusion. Whitbread has above-average pricing power in its segment, high operating leverage, meaningful cost-out and a working freehold-to-buyback loop, offset by financial leverage near its ceiling and a rising base of fixed rent. These features support step 3 of the case (how the change reaches EPS), and they are the reason the cone of outcomes in step 6 is wide in both directions.

Score: 74, set by the Rater. The gearing is structurally strong: almost all costs are fixed, so 1% of UK RevPAR moves PBT by about £17m (about 4% of EPS). Pricing power over the segment and over Travelodge is real (a £7.75 RevPAR premium, and room rates held at 81% occupancy). There is proven cost-out (£83m, £60m, then about £50m a year), a direct-booking data loop and a proceeds-to-buyback loop, and forecast EPS growth is about 3.4 times revenue growth, against a median of about 2. The score is held below the high 70s because financial leverage is near its 3.5x ceiling rather than comfortable, the sale-and-leasebacks add about £100m of inflation-linked fixed rent by FY31, Germany lacks pricing power, and the same gearing has just run in reverse through the cost squeeze.

Evidence and reasoning, year by year.

  • FY27 is a trough year by design. The restaurant exit removes about £160m of F&B revenue; business rates rose £35m in April 2026 and wages rose 4.1%; Germany is around breakeven; interest income has fallen with the cash pile; and the AGP adds £10m of costs. H1 EBITDA of about £600m and H2 EBITDA of about £452m (flat on last year's H2) give full-year EBITDA flat at £1.05bn and PBT of about £412m. That PBT is slightly above the £407m consensus because of the H1 beat and current trading of +3.2% RevPAR.
  • FY28 is the recovery. RevPAR growth of 2% (+£34m), room growth of 2% (+£20m), the AGP (+£45m on FY27) and Germany (+£18m), against net cost inflation of only about £45m (rates frozen, wages +3.9%, £50m of efficiencies), lift EBITDA by £68m to £1.12bn. Below EBITDA, depreciation on new rooms and leaseback assets, the May 2027 bond refinancing and lease interest on the FY27 sale-and-leasebacks absorb about £28m, leaving PBT of about £452m and EPS of 203p, level with consensus.
  • FY29 is where I part from consensus. The same levers (about +£100m gross, less about £35m of costs) give EBITDA of £1.19bn and PBT of about £492m, 6% below the £522m consensus. The sell-side's 11% post-Budget upgrades to FY29 appear to carry the full rates benefit to the bottom line without the lease and interest drag that property recycling creates.
  • FY30 is a stall year on my numbers. I deduct £30m for half of the £65m business rates cliff edge and £6m for visitor levies, so PBT is roughly flat at £503m, while buybacks still lift EPS by 8%.
  • FY31 resumes growth, with PBT of £549m and EPS of 287p, as Germany approaches £55m of profit and the AGP completes.

Scope for double-digit growth, and for higher growth and margins than in the past. EPS compounds at about 12% a year from the FY27 trough to FY31, roughly half from PBT growth and half from a fall of about 15% in the share count through buybacks funded by property sales. The EBITDA margin rises 2 to 2.5 points above FY26 because F&B leaves the mix and the AGP lands. PBT, however, does not regain its FY24 peak (£584m) even by FY31 (about £549m), which is consistent with Bernstein's view and means that the four-year growth is a recovery with a buyback kicker, not a step-change in the earning power of Whitbread's business model.

EPS compounds at about 12% a year from the FY27 trough to FY31: half from PBT growth, half from a 15% fall in the share count. A recovery with a buyback kicker, not a step-change in earning power.

Testing the forecasts. Past delivery makes the FY28 uplift plausible: the restaurants are closed, the efficiency machine is proven, Germany has already turned a profit once, and the rates relief is legislated. The thesis relies on strengths Whitbread demonstrably has (pricing, cost control and share gains) rather than strengths it would need to acquire, except in Germany, where direct distribution is unproven.

  • The cone of outcomes over 18 months is wide: FY28 PBT of £400m to £490m, roughly (12)% to +8% around my base. The cone is skewed slightly positive because the cost lines are now known and the revenue line is running ahead of assumptions.
  • Guidance is more likely to be met or edged up than cut at the next three events, unless STR's weekly hotel data turns down.
  • Consensus for FY27 and FY28 is more likely to drift up than down; FY29 is the year most likely to be trimmed.

Where I differ from the market. I am 2% above consensus for FY27 because of the H1 beat and current trading, evidence the sell-side partly holds. I am level with consensus for FY28. I am 5% below consensus for FY29 and FY30 because of the lease and interest drag of property recycling and the FY30 rates cliff edge, which the sell-side has not modelled.

Conclusion. The forecasts show a trough in FY27, an 11% EPS recovery in FY28 and about 12% compound EPS growth to FY31, with margins modestly above the past but PBT still below the FY24 level (£584m) in FY31. The forecasts support step 3 of the case for FY28 and temper step 6, because the growth comes from recovery and buybacks rather than from higher earning power.

#7Scope for upgrades to guidance, consensus and narrative over 6 to 12 months

Evidence. Much of the good news is already in consensus; five possible upgrades are not.

  • Already in consensus (and so momentum, not scope): the rates freeze (FY28 EPS up 9% in three months), the H1 beat, the Q3 trading update of +3.2% RevPAR, the AGP and Germany FY28 bridges, and Germany's profitability in FY27.

Not yet in consensus or guidance

  1. FY28 cost guidance, to be given in January and April: net cost inflation at or below 3% would sit below the brokers' implicit 3 to 4%.
  2. Any resumption of the buyback: Morgan Stanley alone models it early, and the £2bn shareholder-returns framework implies that buybacks must start by FY28 or FY29.
  3. Travelodge's weakness converting into share gains above the 1 to 2% a year assumed.
  4. The pricing of sale-and-leasebacks at 4.75% yields, which, if sustained, lowers the lease drag below Bernstein's £100m and supports faster deleveraging.
  5. Germany's H2 FY27 profit arriving above the small positive implied, with German Q3 RevPAR +9.5% after a flat Q2.
  • Against: Redburn's expected £10m reversal of H1 cost phasing caps the FY27 upside. Deutsche Bank expects FY27 UK RevPAR growth of 1.5% and has reversed only half of its November 2025 downgrades, the rest reflecting restaurant disruption, German acquisition losses and headwinds at the Middle East joint venture. Corporate negotiated rates are expected to fall 3.5% in 2027.

The scope for estimate upgrades over the next 6 to 12 months is modest in size (FY27 PBT +£5 to 10m, FY28 PBT +£0 to 15m) but reasonably likely in direction. A shift in the narrative from "an asset-heavy hotelier in a cost squeeze" to "a self-funded recovery with cash returns resuming" would change the multiple, not the estimates. My FY29 forecast is below consensus, so I expect FY29 consensus to be trimmed as FY28 is confirmed, which is the normal shape of a recovery year.

So what. Richard should expect a pattern of small beats, held FY27 guidance and an FY28 guide at or slightly above consensus. The buyback is the one announcement that could move the shares disproportionately, because it would validate the property proceeds, the leverage and the five-year plan at once.

#9Riskiness and simplicity of the case

Evidence. The case is simple to track, but it is fragile in several connected ways.

  • Simplicity: the case has one dominant driver (UK RevPAR against a cost base that is now known), two self-help legs (the AGP and Germany) and one financial leg (property proceeds funding buybacks). All of them are reported half-yearly, with a Q3 trading update in January.
  • Fragilities: operating gearing of about 4% of EPS per 1% of RevPAR; lease-adjusted leverage of 3.4x against a 3.5x limit, a BBB- rating and about 5x on a fully capitalised basis, so a bad half-year and slow proceeds could force cuts in capital spending or delay buybacks; three programmes running at once (conversions, German scaling and property recycling), which a former Accor executive calls the main execution risk; and £1.5bn of proceeds required to fund all growth, so slower transactions cascade into every other leg.
  • Further fragilities: 77% of leases are inflation-linked; the FY30 rates cliff edge is up to £65m, or £150m unmitigated by the end of the decade on Redburn's figure; the bond refinancing is at about 6%; AI booking agents could bypass direct booking, the least monitored threat; visitor levies are coming; and German leasehold costs are fixed if the German economy stagnates.
  • Suddenness and trackability: STR's weekly hotel data gives early warning of RevPAR. Half of bookings are made within the week of stay, so visibility is short, but surprises arrive gradually through trading updates rather than as profit warnings. The accounting is clean on adjusted measures, but statutory profit is a fraction of adjusted profit (H1 £109m against £287m) and capitalised interest has tripled, so sceptics will question the quality of earnings.
  • Sector precedents: owner-operator hoteliers suffer badly in demand downturns (Travelodge was "financially impaired for a decade" after its full sale-and-leaseback), and post-pandemic pricing proved cyclical (UK ROCE peaked at 15.5% in FY24 and has fallen since). Morgan Stanley's recession scenario puts PBT at £365m and EPS at 155p on a 12x multiple; Jefferies' downside is 1,900p (32)% on negative RevPAR and an EV/EBIT multiple below 10x.

Inference. The case is simple to state and to track but not low-risk. It is a geared bet that UK consumers, whom the house view rates Double Underweight, keep paying 2% more for budget rooms while a leverage-constrained company executes three programmes at once. Most of the risks (RevPAR, proceeds and leverage) are gradual and trackable; there are two dated step-changes (the May 2027 refinancing and the April 2029 rates cliff edge) and one slow-moving tail risk (AI booking agents bypassing direct booking).

So what. The cone of outcomes is wide: FY28 EPS of plausibly 185p to 215p, and a share price of plausibly 2,000p to 4,000p over 18 months. The skew is positive because the cost side of the cone has narrowed sharply since October while the revenue side is running ahead, but a UK downturn would hit revenue, leverage and the multiple together. The strongest counter-case is Jefferies': low RevPAR growth plus high cost inflation in a capital-intensive model. Jefferies was right for two years, is now wrong on costs, and could still be right on RevPAR.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side majority treats the balance sheet as the binding constraint; I think RevPAR is the binding variable and leverage is the amplifier, which is why I would track STR's weekly data before the leverage ratio. On the environment, the house view's Double Underweight on Consumer discretionary fights this case directly, and I do not dismiss it. The case is congruent with the house environment view only in that it needs no fall in discount rates and Whitbread is a large, liquid, investment-grade company.

Conclusion. The case is simple to track but geared and leverage-constrained, with a wide cone of outcomes skewed modestly positive, and with risks that are gradual rather than sudden except at two dated points. The riskiness weakens step 6 of the case (the downside is real, at roughly (25)%) and is the reason the memo's riskiness rating is a D.

Score: 39, set by the Rater. The case is simple and trackable (one dominant driver, UK RevPAR, with weekly STR data and gradual rather than sudden risks), and the FY28 EPS cone of 185p to 215p is only about (9)% to +6%. However, the case is a geared bet on a consumer the house view rates Double Underweight: about 4% of EPS per 1% of RevPAR, lease-adjusted leverage of 3.4x against a 3.5x limit (net debt/EBITDA 5.0x, 88th percentile), three programmes at once, £1.5bn of proceeds that every leg depends on, and dated risks in the 2027 refinancing and the FY30 rates cliff edge. Sector precedent shows that owner-operators suffer badly in downturns, and the downside is (25) to (32)%. The score sits just above D'Ieteren's leveraged complexity and below Rexel.

#10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Evidence. The dashboard's rule places Whitbread at Turning/Inflecting (26-Nov-26), and the evidence supports that phase.

  • Estimates and earnings: estimates bottomed in autumn 2026 and have risen 5 to 9% over three to six months, after falling 17% over the year. The earnings trough is FY27 (EPS 183p against 207p), with growth resuming in FY28.
  • Price: the share price bottomed at 2,097p (the 52-week low, in spring 2026), is up 22% over six months and stands 13% above its 200-day average. However, the 200-day average has risen in only three of the last twelve months, and the twelve-month return is flat.
  • Positioning and brokers: short interest collapsed from above 10% to 3%; the activist overhang cleared in November; and brokers have moved from Sell and Underperform to Hold with higher targets, rather than to Buy.
  • Valuation: the multiple of 12.6x sits at the 22nd percentile of ten years and the 70th percentile of two years.

Inference. Whitbread's shares have moved from bottoming (spring 2026: a multiple of 10.5 to 11x and short interest above 10%) to turning up (from October 2026: estimates and targets rising, Holds replacing Sells). The shares are not yet in thesis-broadening, which requires Germany's profit to be visible, the FY28 guidance to be given and the buyback to resume; if the case works, broadening arrives between April and October 2027. RevPAR growth below 1.5% in the January update, or FY27 property proceeds below £300m, would signal that the turn is stalling or collapsing.

So what. In turning-up phases the multiple does most of the work, and the next two reports carry disproportionate weight. The risk is that the shares are already 14% above their spring base, so a soft January update would look like a failed turn.

Where I differ from the market. I agree with the dashboard's phase. The sector digest's "Big but not Early" judgement on the property-sale story is fair for the sector as a whole; for Whitbread specifically, the story is early because the buyback has not restarted.

Conclusion. Whitbread is in the Turning/Inflecting phase, past bottoming and short of thesis-broadening, with the broadening tests dated at April and October 2027. The lifecycle phase supports step 5 of the case and sets the frame for the fair multiple in #11.

Score: 68, set by the Rater. I agree with the computed and memo phase of Turning/Inflecting. Estimates bottomed in autumn 2026 and are up 5 to 9%, the activist and short-seller overhangs have cleared, Holds are replacing Sells, FY27 is the earnings trough, and the multiple sits near the bottom of its range: the cause for concern is clearing, early in the Turning Up phase. The stock falls short of Reply because the shares are already up 22% in six months, the rates upgrade is in consensus, and broadening (Germany proven, buyback resumed) is not due before April to October 2027, while a soft January update could look like a failed turn.

#11The fair multiple

My fair multiple is 14.5x for the next 6 to 18 months; the 16.6x guideline is a destination for 2028, once the thesis broadens.

Evidence. The guideline fair multiple for the Turning/Inflecting phase is 16.57x two-year forward earnings (the 60th percentile of the stock's own ten-year history), 31% above today's 12.64x.

  • The ten-year range (outliers removed) runs from 11.0x at the 10th percentile through a 15.5x median and 18.6x at the 75th percentile to 21.9x at the 90th.
  • The history has four regimes: 12 to 16x in 2016 to 2018, as a conglomerate with Costa; 16 to 19x in 2019, as a pure-play hotel company with zero interest rates and a £2.5bn buyback; 22 to 40x in 2020 to 2022, on depressed pandemic earnings; and 10.5 to 13.6x since mid-2024, as costs rose and capital spending intensified.
  • Peers: IHG trades at 24x (its 92nd percentile), Accor at 16x, Scandic at 11x and Melia at 12.6x. Whitbread traded at a 46% discount to asset-light peers in March 2025.
  • Brokers: Deutsche Bank regards 14.9x FY27 earnings as leaving limited room to re-rate; Morgan Stanley's bull case is £50 a share and its bear case uses a 12x P/E; Jefferies applies the low end of the historical range because of weak momentum.

Inference. The 60th-percentile guideline describes a stock the market no longer sees. It is heavily influenced by the 2019 and 2021 to 2023 regimes, when interest rates were near zero, Whitbread had net cash after the Costa sale, and the earnings base was depressed. The 2024 to 2026 regime of 10.5 to 13.6x describes the stock in a cost squeeze with no growth, which the case says is ending. A fair multiple for a Turning/Inflecting owner-operator with an 11% ROIC, 3.4x lease-adjusted leverage, a gilt yield of 5.3% and EPS growth of 11 to 13% sits between the two regimes, at 14 to 15x. That range is the 35th percentile ("conservative") band of 14.0x and a little above, and it is roughly where the shares traded in late 2023, when PBT was last growing.

So what. I take 14.5x as my own fair multiple for the next 6 to 18 months. I treat the 16.57x guideline as a thesis-broadening multiple, which needs Germany proven, buybacks running and FY30's rates cliff edge resolved; reaching it is an 18 to 36 month proposition rather than a 12-month one. On my 24-month-forward EPS of about 216p, the shares trade on 13.0x today, so the guideline implies a 28% re-rating and my 14.5x implies an 11.5% re-rating.

Viewforth fair multiple 14.5x for the next 6 to 18 months (+11.5% re-rating on 13.0x); the 16.6x guideline (+28%) is an 18 to 36 month destination that needs Germany proven, buybacks running and the FY30 rates cliff resolved.

Where I differ from the market. The market's 12.6x says investors do not yet believe the recovery. Deutsche Bank's view of "limited room to re-rate" at 14.9x FY27 earnings applies a one-year multiple to trough earnings, and so overstates the valuation. My view sits between the dashboard's guideline and the sell-side's caution.

Conclusion. The 16.6x guideline is defensible only as a destination once the thesis broadens; a fair multiple for the next 6 to 18 months is about 14.5x, still 11 to 15% above today's multiple. The fair multiple supports step 6 of the case at a reduced size and is the basis for the return arithmetic in #12.

Score: 78, set by the Rater. Cheap on one measure and neutral on the other gives a B. I place the score low in the band because part of the cheapness is deserved: the ten-year history includes zero-rate, net-cash and pandemic-earnings regimes the stock no longer resembles, leverage is near its ceiling with the gilt at 5.3%, and the memo's own fair multiple of 14.5x is only 11 to 15% above today's multiple.

#12Total shareholder return

Over twelve months, the multiple does most of the work; over three years, earnings take over.

The arithmetic over 6 to 18 months (base case, taking twelve months to November 2027).

  • Earnings: the 24-month-forward EPS the market prices today is a blend of FY28 and FY29, about 216p on my forecasts (consensus about 222p), so today's multiple on my numbers is 13.0x. In twelve months the window rolls to FY29 and FY30, about 238p on my forecasts, so earnings growth contributes +10%.
  • Multiple: +28% at the 16.57x guideline; +11.5% at my 14.5x.
  • Dividends: 97p, a 3.5% yield.
  • Total at the guideline: 1.10 × 1.28 = 1.41, plus the 3.5% dividend, gives about +44% (a share price of about 3,940p).
  • Total at my 14.5x: 1.10 × 1.115 = 1.23, plus 3.5%, gives about +26% (a share price of about 3,450p).
  • Total at an unchanged 13.0x: EPS growth plus the dividend gives about +13.5%.

Over three years (to November 2029). The 24-month-forward EPS rolls to FY31 and FY32, about 298p on my forecasts (assuming FY32 growth of 8%), which is +38% on today's 216p, or 11% a year. Dividends add about 11% cumulatively.

  • At 16.57x, the share price is about 4,940p (+76%; total return about +87%, or 23% a year).
  • At 14.5x, the share price is about 4,320p (+54%; total return about +65%, or 18% a year).
  • At an unchanged 13.0x, the share price is about 3,870p (+38%; total return about +49%, or 14% a year).

At the guideline multiple, earnings drive roughly half of the three-year return (about a third of that earnings growth comes from buybacks) and the multiple drives the other half; at my fair multiple, earnings drive about three-quarters.

What drives the return. The earnings leg depends on RevPAR growth of 2% and the FY28 uplift (judgements 1 to 3 in #0); the buyback leg depends on property proceeds and leverage (judgement 4); and the multiple leg depends on the narrative turning, which the January and April reports decide. The FY30 rates cliff edge (judgement 5) is the main threat to the three-year earnings leg and to the guideline multiple.

The probability-weighted 18-month return (to May 2028) is about +22%.

  • Base (50%): FY28 EPS delivered near 203p; FY29 consensus trimmed towards my 229p; RevPAR growth of 2%; proceeds of £400m or more; the buyback resumed at £100m. Forward EPS of about 255p on a 14.0x multiple gives a share price of about 3,570p, +27%, plus 5% of dividends: +32%.
  • Better (20%): RevPAR growth of 3% or more; Germany at £25m or more in FY28; proceeds at 4.75% yields; a £250m buyback early. The market pays the 16.5x guideline on forward EPS of about 275p, for a share price of about 4,540p, +62%, plus 5%: +67%.
  • Worse (30%): the UK consumer weakens; RevPAR is flat to negative in FY28; PBT is about £400m in FY28 and about £420m in FY29; the buyback is deferred; leverage sits at 3.5x. Forward EPS of about 195p at 11x (the ten-year 10th percentile) gives a share price of about 2,145p, (23)%, plus 4% of dividends: (19)%. Jefferies' 1,900p downside (32)% marks the tail.
  • Weighted: 0.5 × 32% + 0.2 × 67% + 0.3 × (19)% = +22% over 18 months, about 14% a year, with a two-to-one ratio of upside to downside and a 30% chance of a loss.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side's median target of 2,861p (+2%) says it sees the shares as fairly valued on trough earnings and a trough multiple; the mean target of 3,023p and Morgan Stanley's 3,200p are closer to my 14.5x case. The market's return expectation is low because its multiple expectation is static, and the case rests on that multiple expectation changing.

Conclusion. The base return is about +26% over twelve months at my fair multiple and about +44% at the guideline; the probability-weighted return is about +22% over 18 months; and the three-year return is 14 to 23% a year, driven half by earnings recovery and buybacks and half by re-rating. The return supports step 6 of the case as a positively skewed but not asymmetric reward, with the downside at about (20) to (25)%.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. A return of about +22% sits just above the B floor, which maps to about 77. The three-year check is supportive. I hold the score at 76 because the lower tail is fat (a 30% chance of (19)%, and Jefferies' (32)% case) and correlated with leverage, and because about half of the central return rests on a re-rating rather than on earnings. #13Summary conclusion

A cost trough, not a demand trough: the case pays about +22% probability-weighted over 18 months with a two-to-one skew, but a weak UK consumer and 3.4x lease-adjusted leverage keep the downside real at (20) to (25)%.

Whitbread is a high-quality UK hotel operator inside a capital-heavy model. Its two-year cost squeeze has been ended by legislation, and its self-help has already been executed on the ground. FY27 is therefore a visible earnings trough, FY28 is a guided recovery of about 11% in EPS, and the shares trade at 12.6x two-year forward earnings, near the bottom of their ten-year range, with estimates, targets and ratings turning up since October 2026.

The case is a cause for concern clearing in a quality cyclical at trough-on-trough, with a probability-weighted 18-month return of about +22% and a two-to-one skew. The case's weakness is that Whitbread's trough is a cost trough rather than a demand trough: a weak UK consumer and 3.4x lease-adjusted leverage keep the downside real at (20) to (25)%, and the 16.6x guideline multiple is a destination for 2028 rather than for 2027.

What to watch, in order:

  1. STR's weekly midscale and economy RevPAR data and the Q3 update on 13-Jan-27, with UK RevPAR growth of 2% or better and FY28 net cost inflation of 3% or less as the pass marks;
  2. the FY27 results on 27-Apr-27, for FY28 PBT guidance at or above £450m, property proceeds of £400m or more, lease-adjusted leverage of 3.3x or below, and any buyback announcement;
  3. the H1 FY28 results in October 2027, for adjusted PBT above £310m, Germany in profit for the half, and the extension rooms trading;
  4. sale-and-leaseback yields holding near 4.75 to 5.5% against a 5.3% gilt yield;
  5. Germany's direct-booking share and brand awareness (22% in August 2026) against its reliance on online travel agents;
  6. the November 2027 and 2028 Budgets, for any extension of the rates freeze beyond FY29;
  7. Travelodge's quarterly RevPAR, as the read-across on competitive weakness.

The four overall ratings

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 64, set by the Rater. The input forces are clearly positive: a modest external net tailwind from legislated cost relief and weak rivals (60), and a large, mostly executed self-help programme (67). However, the forces reach profits only as about 12% EPS growth from a trough, near the Universe median, with half of that growth from buybacks. Part of the force is a policy windfall that expires in FY29, so the change is real but lifts profits only to typical growth, which the levels place in the low to mid 60s.
Foundations' Robustness: 62, set by the Rater. The UK operating franchise is robust: brand leadership, direct distribution, a consolidating segment and a £5.5 to 6.4bn freehold estate (quality 61). Short-term delivery is reliable, but the medium-term record is being rebuilt after a plan reset (57). The foundations are held below the 75 band by cyclical, discretionary demand, an 11% ROIC with poor returns on a decade of growth capital spending, and leverage at its ceiling. These are not the stable, non-discretionary attributes that lift CVS Group despite ordinary returns.
Setups' Fit/Crispness: 66, set by the Rater. The case fits a cause for concern clearing in a quality cyclical at trough-on-trough. The concerns (the cost squeeze, the activist, the restaurant losses and the German losses) are visibly clearing, and FY27 is a clear earnings trough. One element is loose: the trough is in costs, not demand, so a second trough is possible. The quality label is also contested by the capital-heavy model and the shift to leasehold. Current problems (proceeds lagging, leverage at its limit) blur the fit further, so the setup sits in the 65 to 75 range Richard gives a major cause for concern clearing in a middling-quality business, at the lower end of that range.
Case Riskiness: 38, set by the Rater. One dominant, weekly-trackable driver and gradual risks keep the case simple. But operating gearing of about 4% of EPS per 1% of RevPAR, on a consumer the house view rates Double Underweight, combined with leverage at its ceiling and a dependence on property proceeds, means a demand miss would hit earnings, the balance sheet and the multiple together. The downside of (25) to (32)% is too large for the paper-cut risk profile that earns 75 or more.

End notes

Sources and dates. The Analyst's memo and forecast inputs; the Financial Analyst's model (update 1); FactSet financials and consensus; and the Master Dashboard (valuation and price charts). The latest Earnings Review on file is dated 26-Nov-26 and covers the H1 FY27 results (the 26 weeks to 27-Aug-26, reported on 13-Oct-26). The FactSet financials' last reported period is also August 2026, so no results have been reported since, and the Earnings Review's figures are the latest. The four standard reports are the Change Forces report (26-Nov-26), the Business Foundations report (4-Aug-26, now more than three months old), the Leadership Foundations report (26-Nov-26) and the Risks report (26-Nov-26). Library visuals are drawn from the figures in the memo; default visuals were made on 27-Nov-26.

Bases of the figures. Earnings, EPS and PBT in the memo are the company's adjusted figures (post-IFRS 16, excluding adjusting items); FY26 adjusted EPS was 207p and adjusted PBT £483m. The Financial Analyst's model shows history on FactSet's reported basis (for example FY26 pre-tax profit of £473.8m and EPS of 2.34 GBP), so its history lines do not match the adjusted figures.

The model's split of the return. The split in #12 is on the return's own basis: the two-year-forward P/E and two-year-forward EPS, today against each horizon. The multiple and earnings parts multiply (one plus the first, times one plus the second, less one, gives the change in the share price), and dividends add to that. The template's own split (TSR Dupont sheet, rows 46 and 47) measures the same return on trailing twelve-month earnings and the trailing multiple: at the 18-month column, +69.5% from the multiple and (10.8)% from earnings; at the three-year column, +77.7% from the multiple and +6.9% from earnings. The template's split reads differently when earnings over the next twelve months are flat or falling, so the split in #12 is the one to use. The model's two horizons are its fixed columns after the last reported period, so they end on the dates shown, not 18 months and three years from today.

Editorial notes. The return at my 14.5x fair multiple appeared in the source as both +27% (#0) and +26% (#12); this page uses +26%, which the arithmetic in #12 gives. The memo gives Premier Inn's Q3 RevPAR growth as +3.2% (the first five weeks of Whitbread's Q3) and as +2.3% (the quarter compared with Travelodge's +0.4%); the source does not reconcile the two periods. In #10, the shares are described as 14% above their spring base, although the 2,804p price is about 34% above the 2,097p spring low; the 14% matches the three-month return. Neither figure could be checked against the Financial Analyst's model, so both are left as written.
